ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the figure is triangle ABC, BC is the horizontal base, and A is above. Inside the figure there are two rectangular top edges parallel to the base: the lower horizontal edge is labeled 5, and the corresponding vertical height is labeled 1; the higher horizontal edge is labeled 3, and the corresponding vertical height is labeled 2. Reasoning: Let the height of the triangle from A to BC be H, and the length of base BC be L. In the triangle, the width of a horizontal cross-section parallel to the base decreases linearly with height, so the width at height y from BC is w(y)=L(1-y/H). From the figure, w(1)=5, therefore L(1-1/H)=5; also w(2)=3, therefore L(1-2/H)=3. Subtracting the two equations gives L/H=2, so L=2H. Substitute into the first equation: 2H(1-1/H)=5, that is 2H-2=5, so H=7/2.

method.method_draft: Use a width-vs-height linear model for horizontal slices of the triangle. From the diagram, read that the rectangle labeled 5 has height 1 above base BC, and the rectangle labeled 3 has height 2 above base BC; their top horizontal sides span the triangle at those heights. Let the triangle altitude from A to BC be H and let the base length be L. By similarity of horizontal cross-sections in a triangle, the available width at height y above BC is L(1-y/H). Thus set L(1-1/H)=5 and L(1-2/H)=3. Subtract or solve the two equations to get H=7/2.

method.method_draft: Use two nested similar triangles above the rectangles. From the diagram, the horizontal segment of length 3 is one unit higher than the horizontal segment of length 5, because the rectangles have heights 2 and 1 above BC. Let x be the vertical distance from A down to the length-3 segment. Then the distance from A down to the length-5 segment is x+1.
